(1) HIV patients with AIDS have a high prevalence of subclinical adrenal insufficiency, which can be reversed by administration of low doses of hydrocortisone; (2) the majority of patients with AIDS have increased sensitivity of their adrenal glands to glucocorticoid feedback, which may contribute to adrenal insufficiency in these patients; (3) patients with AIDS have decreased sensitivity of their adrenal cortex to ACTH, which may contribute, at least partially, to adrenal insuff

the HIV-1 infection and its treatment with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) are associated with abnormalities of the HPA axis that may contribute to the morbidity and mortality of HIV-infected persons and that the HPA axis abnormalities associated with HIV infection and/or HAART may be mediated by acquired hypersensitivity/resistance of target tissues to glucocorticoid action.

1) the HPA axis may be abnormal in the early stages of HIV infection, 2) the HPA abnormalities may be associated with antiretroviral medications and 3) the HPA disturbances may be associated with the HIV infection itself.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the etiology of HPA abnormalities, and the role they play in the pathogenesis of HIV disease.
the role of the HPA axis in the development of HIV disease, the role of glucocorticoids in HIV pathogenesis and the development of novel therapies for HIV disease based on glucocorticoid analogs.
the study of the HPA axis in the setting of HIV disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the HPA axis is dysfunctional in HIV-infected patients, with the degree of dysfunction being related to the stage of the disease, the presence of opportunistic infections, and the use of antiviral medications.

HPA axis abnormalities are not a major cause of morbidity or mortality in HIV infection and that the most important clinical manifestations of HPA dysfunction are the consequences of the use of corticosteroids for treatment of opportunistic infections.
HPA axis abnormalities in HIV infection are common but are usually mild, subclinical or transient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are many potential etiologies of HPA dysfunction in HIV infection and that these abnormalities are often reversible with proper treatment.

HPA abnormalities are common in HIV infection and that the most important etiologic considerations in HIV patients are the medications administered to treat infections as well as the HIV infection itself.
HPA axis disturbances are common in the HIV infected and that these abnormalities can have significant clinical consequences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HIV infection is not associated with a specific HPA axis dysfunction, but rather with a wide variety of disturbances, which are likely multifactorial.

HIV infection and disease is associated with a broad spectrum of HPA abnormalities ranging from subclinical alterations to frank adrenal insensitivity and/or adrenal insufficiency and that clinicians should be aware of the possibility of HPA axis abnormalities in HIV patients.

HIV infection and disease is associated with a spectrum of abnormalities of the HPA axis ranging from subtle subclinical alterations in tissue sensitivity/resistance to glucorticoids to frank adrenal insuficiency.
